ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> The sample collected by Byrd et al. (2023) consisted of 102 English-speaking monolingual participants (57 women, 38 men, 7 undisclosed; M age = 30.4 years) recruited on the Prolific platform (app.prolific.co), who were compensated for their participation at an expected rate of $9.85/hour.

> Specifically, we asked whether a trial's deliberation dynamics could predict whether the participant gave the correct response or the intuitive, biased response.

> The original data were collected under a protocol approved by the Office for Human Subjects Protection at Florida State University (STUDY00000697), and all participants gave informed consent in the original study. reasoning effort from none ("GPT -no forced-zero rule") through low, medium, and high ("GPT -low reasoning," "GPT -medium reasoning," and "GPT -high reasoning").

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1278 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1275), temporary files (3). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 990 columns across 58 data files.
#### Issues Identified

138 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 58 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: The sample collected by Byrd et al. (2023) consisted of 102 English-speaking monolingual participants (57 women, 38 men, 7 undisclosed; M age = 30.4 years) recruited on the Prolific platform (app.prolific.co), who were compensated for their participation at an expected rate of $9.85/hour.
Specifically, we asked whether a trial's deliberation dynamics could predict whether the participant gave the correct response or the intuitive, biased response.

The original data were collected under a protocol approved by the Office for Human Subjects Protection at Florida State University (STUDY00000697), and all participants gave informed consent in the original study. reasoning effort from none ("GPT -no forced-zero rule") through low, medium, and high ("GPT -low reasoning," "GPT -medium reasoning," and "GPT -high reasoning").

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("main_analyses.Rmd", "prompt_optimization_analysis.rmd", 
"Tell Us What You Really Think WIDE with interrater agreement.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("none", "none", 
"none")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **1 data path was built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `thinkaloudreflectiontestexperiment1-cleanedwiththinkalouddata.xlsx`, `thinkaloudreflectionteststudy2-cleanedwiththinkalouddata.xlsx`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 1 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("main_analyses.Rmd", "prompt_optimization_analysis.rmd", 
"Tell Us What You Really Think WIDE with interrater agreement.R"
), Outcome = c("errored", "ran_ok", "errored"), Detail = c("runtime", 
"", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(25.2, 50.9, 5.5)), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

18 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

info.title: Rhythm of Thought: Tracing the Dynamics of Deliberation in Reasoning

author.affiliation:
CNRS
								Université Paris Cité
								
									46 rue Saint-Jacques
									F-75005
									Paris

text.text: When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to reason further.
But what people do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes helps remain unclear.

We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort) and expressed confidence.
Deliberation showed a temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation grew as reasoning progressed.
Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items.
Confidence and deliberation showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted increases in confidence.
Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.
The human capacity to deliberate and engage in deep reflection has long been regarded as a defining feature of human cognition.

It also sits at the heart of the highly influential dualprocess theories that characterize human reasoning as an interplay between fast, intuitive processing ("System 1") and slow, effortful deliberation ("System 2"; Evans & Stanovich, 2013; Kahneman, 2011).
text.formatted: It also sits at the heart of the highly influential dualprocess theories that characterize human reasoning as an interplay between fast, intuitive processing ("System 1") and slow, effortful deliberation ("System 2"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Evans & Stanovich, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kahneman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its prominence, deliberation itself remains something of a "black box" (De Neys, 2025; Myers & Chater, 2024).
text.formatted: Despite its prominence, deliberation itself remains something of a "black box" <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(De Neys, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Myers & Chater, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One reason is that it encompasses multiple distinct functions (De Neys, 2025).
text.formatted: One reason is that it encompasses multiple distinct functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(De Neys, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Sometimes we deliberate to work out an answer, as when computing each person's share of a dinner bill.
At other times, the answer is already in hand, and we deliberate to defend it, as when searching for the argument that will convince a friend to see the movie we prefer.
In other cases, we deliberate to keep a response in check, as when stopping short of giving away a surprise we'd promised to keep.
And we can even deliberate about our reasoning itself, as when deciding how hard to study for tomorrow's exam and when to stop.

Generating a response, justifying it, controlling it, and regulating the effort spent on it are each well-known and studied in their own right, yet surprisingly little is known about how prevalent they are or how they combine when people reason.
This functional decomposition raises several questions about how deliberation unfolds during reasoning.
At the most basic level, correct and biased responses may differ simply because biased reasoners deliberate less.

Yet biased reasoners often also deliberate, sometimes at length, which has been interpreted as justification of their initial response (Evans & Wason, 1976; Mercier & Sperber, 2011; Pennycook et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Yet biased reasoners often also deliberate, sometimes at length, which has been interpreted as justification of their initial response <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Evans & Wason, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Mercier & Sperber, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Pennycook et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Accuracy may therefore depend not only on how much people deliberate, but on which functions they engage.

The temporal organization of these functions may matter as well. Evans (2019), for example, proposed that reasoners first deliberate to justify their initial response and generate an alternative only when this justification fails, a proposal that has yet to receive direct empirical support; alternatively, generation may precede justification, with reasoners first working out a candidate response before evaluating it.
text.formatted: The temporal organization of these functions may matter as well. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Evans (2019)</ref>, for example, proposed that reasoners first deliberate to justify their initial response and generate an alternative only when this justification fails, a proposal that has yet to receive direct empirical support; alternatively, generation may precede justification, with reasoners first working out a candidate response before evaluating it.

text.text: This question of ordering is not limited to generation and justification.
Control, too, may be recruited early, to keep an intuitive response in check while deliberation proceeds, or only later, once an alternative has been generated.
Such differences in temporal organization may themselves distinguish correct from biased reasoning.

Finally, metareasoning accounts, which describe how people monitor and regulate their own thinking, propose that low confidence recruits further deliberation, which may in turn alter confidence (Ackerman & Thompson, 2017; De Neys, 2023).
text.formatted: Finally, metareasoning accounts, which describe how people monitor and regulate their own thinking, propose that low confidence recruits further deliberation, which may in turn alter confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ackerman & Thompson, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">De Neys, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Whether this feedback loop operates similarly across the different functions of deliberation remains largely unknown.
Understanding these dynamics is important not only theoretically, but also practically.

Interventions designed to improve reasoning often treat deliberation as a single quantity to increase, and largely ignore the dynamics of the reasoning process itself (Enke et al., 2023; Isler & Yilmaz, 2023; Sirota, Theodoropoulou, et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Interventions designed to improve reasoning often treat deliberation as a single quantity to increase, and largely ignore the dynamics of the reasoning process itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Enke et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Isler & Yilmaz, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Sirota, Theodoropoulou, et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If deliberation encompasses distinct functions, however, effective interventions may depend on engaging the right function at the right time (De Neys, 2025).
text.formatted: If deliberation encompasses distinct functions, however, effective interventions may depend on engaging the right function at the right time <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(De Neys, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Knowing which functions are engaged during accurate reasoning, and when they appear, would indicate what such training should target.
More broadly, a framework for characterizing the temporal organization of human deliberation may also provide a way to analyze and improve reasoning in artificial systems.

Large language models (LLMs), machine-learning systems trained on vast amounts of text, now generate extended reasoning traces before answering, although these traces need not reflect the underlying computation (Turpin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Large language models (LLMs), machine-learning systems trained on vast amounts of text, now generate extended reasoning traces before answering, although these traces need not reflect the underlying computation <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Turpin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Better characterizing how their reasoning is structured (e.g., which functions analogous to human deliberation they engage in and when; Brady et al., 2025; Kargupta et al., 2025) may help both to make their outputs more interpretable and to improve their performance.
text.formatted: Better characterizing how their reasoning is structured (e.g., which functions analogous to human deliberation they engage in and when; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brady et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kargupta et al., 2025)</ref> may help both to make their outputs more interpretable and to improve their performance.

text.text: One major empirical hurdle in addressing these questions is how deliberation is typically measured.
Many studies rely on response time, using slower responses as a proxy for more sustained deliberation (Pennycook et al., 2015; Thompson & Johnson, 2014).
text.formatted: Many studies rely on response time, using slower responses as a proxy for more sustained deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Pennycook et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Thompson & Johnson, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Others use accuracy (Enke et al., 2023; Isler & Yilmaz, 2023), or changes of mind in two-response paradigms-where participants give a fast, initial response before giving a final one after having time to reflect-treating revisions as evidence that deliberation has been engaged (Sirota et al., 2023; Thompson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Others use accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Enke et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Isler & Yilmaz, 2023)</ref>, or changes of mind in two-response paradigms-where participants give a fast, initial response before giving a final one after having time to reflect-treating revisions as evidence that deliberation has been engaged <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sirota et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Thompson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Useful as they are, such measures capture only the amount or outcome of deliberation, not the processes that produce it, and none of them can be mapped unambiguously onto underlying processing (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; van den Berg et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Useful as they are, such measures capture only the amount or outcome of deliberation, not the processes that produce it, and none of them can be mapped unambiguously onto underlying processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">van den Berg et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Characterizing the rhythm of deliberation therefore requires a method that tracks reasoning as it unfolds.

Concurrent think-aloud protocols, where participants verbalize their thoughts while solving a problem (Ericsson & Simon, 1980), provide this more direct access, and have long been used in reasoning research to reveal the processes behind a reasoner's strategy and accuracy (Byrd et al., 2023; Evans et al., 1983), without affecting their performance (Byrd et al., 2023; Fox et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Concurrent think-aloud protocols, where participants verbalize their thoughts while solving a problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ericsson & Simon, 1980)</ref>, provide this more direct access, and have long been used in reasoning research to reveal the processes behind a reasoner's strategy and accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Byrd et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Evans et al., 1983)</ref>, without affecting their performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Byrd et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fox et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Although analyzing verbal protocols has traditionally been slow and labor-intensive, requiring trained raters to code transcripts by hand, LLMs offer a way to overcome this bottleneck.

LLMs are increasingly used across the behavioral and social sciences to analyze text data (Beucler, Purcell, Charles, & De Neys, 2026; Feuerriegel et al., 2025) and, once validated against human raters, can annotate verbal reports at scale (Anlló et al., 2025; Fuławka et al., 2026; Wurgaft et al., 2025).
text.formatted: LLMs are increasingly used across the behavioral and social sciences to analyze text data <ref type="bibr">(Beucler, Purcell, Charles, & De Neys, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Feuerriegel et al., 2025)</ref> and, once validated against human raters, can annotate verbal reports at scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anlló et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fuławka et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Wurgaft et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we used this approach to trace the rhythm of deliberation.

We analyzed the library of think-aloud recordings collected by Byrd et al. (2023) on the verbal Cognitive Reflection Test (vCRT; Sirota, Dewberry, et al., 2021), a set of reasoning problems that pit a tempting intuitive response against the correct answer.
text.formatted: We analyzed the library of think-aloud recordings collected by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al. (2023)</ref> on the verbal Cognitive Reflection <ref type="bibr">Test (vCRT;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Sirota, Dewberry, et al., 2021)</ref>, a set of reasoning problems that pit a tempting intuitive response against the correct answer.

text.text: Such problems have been the main test bed of dual-process research (Frederick, 2005; Pennycook et al., 2016; Stupple et al., 2017), and have shaped much of its theorizing (De Neys, 2023; Evans & Stanovich, 2013).
text.formatted: Such problems have been the main test bed of dual-process research <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Frederick, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Pennycook et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Stupple et al., 2017)</ref>, and have shaped much of its theorizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(De Neys, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Evans & Stanovich, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: We transcribed each recording with automatic speech recognition and used an LLM to segment the transcripts into chunks (i.e., segments expressing a single thought).

Each chunk was then scored for the extent to which it reflected each of the four deliberation functions of interest (generation, justification, control, and regulation), and for the confidence the participant expressed while producing it (see Methods for the definitions supplied to the model, which follow De Neys, 2025).

After validating these scores against human raters, we used statistical modeling to ask how each function unfolds across a verbalization, whether the resulting trajectories differ between correct and biased responses, whether they can predict accuracy, and how confidence and each function are associated with one another from one chunk to the next.
This allowed us to open the black box of deliberation.

The sample collected by Byrd et al. (2023) consisted of 102 English-speaking monolingual participants (57 women, 38 men, 7 undisclosed; M age = 30.4 years) recruited on the Prolific platform (app.prolific.co), who were compensated for their participation at an expected rate of $9.85/hour.
text.formatted: The sample collected by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al. (2023)</ref> consisted of 102 English-speaking monolingual participants (57 women, 38 men, 7 undisclosed; M age = 30.4 years) recruited on the Prolific platform (app.prolific.co), who were compensated for their participation at an expected rate of $9.85/hour.

text.text: Participants solved the 10 items of the vCRT (Sirota, Dewberry, et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Participants solved the 10 items of the vCRT <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sirota, Dewberry, et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Each item cues an intuitive but biased response, yet with verbal rather than mathematical content (e.g., "Would it be ethical for a man to marry the sister of his widow?"
; biased response: either "yes" or "no"; correct response: "Not possible, because he is dead").

Items were presented in a fixed order, and participants typed their answer in a free-response box. Byrd et al. (2023) administered a classic concurrent think-aloud protocol online through the Phonic audio-survey platform.
text.formatted: Items were presented in a fixed order, and participants typed their answer in a free-response box. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al. (2023)</ref> administered a classic concurrent think-aloud protocol online through the Phonic audio-survey platform.

text.text: Participants first practiced thinking aloud before solving each vCRT item while verbalizing their thoughts continuously, with regular reminders to keep talking; a separate audio recording was captured for each item, yielding 1,020 recordings (102 participants × 10 items).
As shown by Byrd et al. (2023) in their original experiment (Study 1), thinking aloud did not affect vCRT accuracy compared to a silent control condition.
text.formatted: As shown by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al. (2023)</ref> in their original experiment (Study 1), thinking aloud did not affect vCRT accuracy compared to a silent control condition.

text.text: We processed the recordings in three automated steps, followed by a validation step (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We processed the recordings in three automated steps, followed by a validation step (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Each recording was first transcribed from speech to text, with every word receiving a timestamp.
An LLM then segmented each transcript into chunks (corresponding to coherent thoughts or reasoning steps).
Finally, an LLM scored every chunk on the four deliberation functions, on confidence, and on two auxiliary dimensions: repetition of the question text and answer selection.
These scores were then validated against human raters.
The resulting corpus of time-stamped, scored chunks forms the input to all subsequent analyses.

Our analysis of deliberation over time required precise timing information for each verbalization.
We transcribed each recording using the open-source automatic speechrecognition pipeline WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023), with the Whisper large-v3-turbo model (Radford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We transcribed each recording using the open-source automatic speechrecognition pipeline WhisperX <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bain et al., 2023)</ref>, with the Whisper large-v3-turbo model <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We then used a wav2vec 2.0 model (Baevski et al., 2020) to align the transcript to the audio, giving every word a start and end time.
text.formatted: We then used a wav2vec 2.0 model <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baevski et al., 2020)</ref> to align the transcript to the audio, giving every word a start and end time.

text.text: We then used GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, 2025; version gpt-5.1-2025-11-13, queried in February 2026 via OpenAI's API) to segment each transcript into chunks, defined as "a coherent idea, thought, or step in the participant's reasoning or verbal expression-including hesitations, repetitions, or meta-comments" (see Supplementary Material 1 for the full prompt).
To minimize variability in the model's outputs, we set temperature, which controls sampling randomness, to 0 and top-p, which controls the range of tokens considered during sampling, to 1.

Drawing on the reasoning literature, De Neys (2025) identified four core functions of deliberation: response generation, response justification, response control, and regulation, hereafter generation, justification, control, and regulation.
To score each deliberation function with the LLM, we adapted De Neys's (2025) descriptions into scoring definitions (see Table 1).
text.formatted: To score each deliberation function with the LLM, we adapted De Neys's (2025) descriptions into scoring definitions (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Deliberation function Definition supplied to the LLM Generation "Refers to actively generating new answers through the deliberate computation or mental simulation of solutions to a given problem.
It often involves hypothetical thinking, algorithmic reasoning, or systematically working through steps to find solutions to a problem."
Justification "Refers to deliberately seeking explicit reasons, arguments, or rationalizations to support or scrutinize generated answers.
It entails building explanations that clarify, validate, or invalidate one's judgments.
It often involves giving reasons, referencing evidence, or explaining why an option makes sense or not."
Control "Refers to deliberately inhibiting, stopping, or correcting a response judged inappropriate (e.g., self-interruption, "wait/but/actually", rejecting an impulsive answer).
A brief "no/stop" alone is not sufficient unless it clearly halts/corrects an emerging response."
Regulation "Refers to deliberately monitoring and managing one's own cognitive processes by allocating effort and resources strategically.
It often involves reflective decisions about continuing or stopping deliberation, adjusting cognitive investment, or evaluating progress and coherence."
We then scored each chunk on the four deliberation functions, using these definitions.
We again used GPT-5.1 to rate each chunk on a continuous scale from 0 (Not at all present) to 100 (Extremely present) for each function.
We set the reasoning effort, which controls how much internal reasoning the model applies to each request, to low.
All four functions were rated within a single prompt, which stated that they "are distinct, but not mutually exclusive."
Alongside the chunk, the model received the vCRT item and its correct and biased answers.
Crucially, to prevent information leakage, the model received neither the rest of the verbalization nor the answer ultimately given by the participant.

For scoring, we instead set the temperature parameter to 1 to allow variation across outputs, obtained eight independent ratings, and averaged them to reduce rating noise (see Le Mens et al., 2023, for a similar approach).
text.formatted: For scoring, we instead set the temperature parameter to 1 to allow variation across outputs, obtained eight independent ratings, and averaged them to reduce rating noise (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Le Mens et al., 2023</ref>, for a similar approach).

text.text: Table 2 shows representative chunks scored on each deliberation function.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref> shows representative chunks scored on each deliberation function.

text.text: We also scored confidence (0 = Not confident at all,100 = Extremely confident): the model was asked to "estimate how confident the speaker sounds in this passage -based on how committed they seem to their ideas, how certain they appear, and whether they express doubt or hesitation."

For this rating, the model received the chunk text alone, without the vCRT item or its answers, so that the confidence scores would track confidence rather than the actual correctness of the verbalized response.

For brevity, we refer to the confidence score extracted from participants' verbalizations as confidence throughout the article, although it may differ from conventional confidence ratings used in psychological experiments.
All LLM-scoring prompts can be found in Supplementary Material 1.

To validate the LLM scoring of the four deliberation functions and of confidence, seven raters (the two authors and five fellow researchers working on reasoning and dual-process theories) independently scored 99 chunks drawn from the corpus.
Chunks were sampled by stratifying on the LLM scores, so as to cover the full range of each dimension.

Mirroring the information given to the model, raters first scored confidence from the chunk text alone, and then the four deliberation functions with the item and its answers displayed, following written instructions matching the LLM prompts, apart from a slightly broader definition of control for the LLM (see Supplementary Material 2 for the full instructions).
Raters were blind to the LLM scores and to the participant's final response.
We assessed interrater reliability with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs; two-way model, consistency type, average measures) to measure the reliability of the mean rating for each dimension.

Reliability was moderate to excellent (Koo & Li, 2016) across dimensions: generation, ICC = .86, 95% CI [.82, .90]; justification, ICC = .87, 95% CI [.83, .91]; control, ICC = .74, 95% CI [.65, .81]; regulation, ICC = .85, 95% CI [.80, .89]; and confidence, ICC = .92, 95% CI [.90, .94].
text.formatted: Reliability was moderate to excellent <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Koo & Li, 2016)</ref> across dimensions: generation, ICC = .86, 95% CI [.82, .90]; justification, ICC = .87, 95% CI [.83, .91]; control, ICC = .74, 95% CI [.65, .81]; regulation, ICC = .85, 95% CI [.80, .89]; and confidence, ICC = .92, 95% CI [.90, .94].

text.text: These averaged human ratings served as a benchmark for selecting the scoring configuration, that is, the model, the prompt, and the reasoning-effort setting.

We compared two LLMs: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024; accessed via Hugging Face's inference API) and GPT-5.1, as well as several prompt variants and, for GPT-5.1, several reasoning-effort settings.
text.formatted: We compared two LLMs: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Grattafiori et al., 2024</ref>; accessed via Hugging Face's inference API) and GPT-5.1, as well as several prompt variants and, for GPT-5.1, several reasoning-effort settings.

text.text: We retained the GPT-5.1 configuration with low reasoning effort because it achieved agreement with human ratings comparable to the best-performing settings at substantially lower cost.
This configuration was used to score the full think-aloud corpus.
The full model-and prompt-comparison results are reported in Supplementary Material 2.

The averaged ratings of the retained configuration correlated strongly with the human averages: Spearman's ρ = .74, 95% CI [.63, .82] for generation, ρ = .76, 95% CI [.66, .83] for justification, ρ = .65, 95% CI [.51, .75] for control, ρ = .83, 95% CI [.76, .88] for regulation, and ρ = .81, 95% CI [.72, .87] for confidence (all ps < .001).
text.formatted: The averaged ratings of the retained configuration correlated strongly with the human averages: Spearman's ρ = .74, 95% CI [.63, .82] for generation, ρ = .76, 95% CI [.66, .83] for justification, ρ = .65, 95% CI [.51, .75] for control, ρ = .83, 95% CI [.76, .88] for regulation, and ρ = .81, 95% CI [.72, .87] for confidence (all ps < .001).

text.text: Finally, the LLM scores, averaged within each trial across chunks (i.e., averaged per participant's verbalization for a given vCRT item), converged with the two trial-level indicators hand-coded by Byrd et al. (2023): whether the participant verbally reconsidered their initial response, and whether they verbalized reasons for or against a response.

(2023)</ref>: whether the participant verbally reconsidered their initial response, and whether they verbalized reasons for or against a response.

text.text: Control correlated most strongly with coded reconsideration of the initial response, ρ = .42, 95% CI [.36, .49], as did regulation, ρ = .38, 95% CI [.31, .45], whereas justification correlated most strongly with coded verbalization of reasons, ρ = .66, 95% CI [.61, .70], all ps < .001.

text.text: The full correlation matrix is reported in Supplementary Material 2.

Confidence scores also reproduced a wellestablished property of explicit confidence ratings: mean confidence within each trial correlated negatively with response time (i.e., the total duration of the trial verbalization), r = -.20, 95% CI [-.28, -.12], p < .001.
text.formatted: Confidence scores also reproduced a wellestablished property of explicit confidence ratings: mean confidence within each trial correlated negatively with response time (i.e., the total duration of the trial verbalization), r = -.20, 95% CI [-.28, -.12], p < .001.

text.text: For comparison, this estimate is similar in magnitude to the average within-participant correlation between confidence and response time reported across 4,089 participants from 76 datasets in the Confidence Database (Rahnev et al., 2020), r = -.24.
text.formatted: For comparison, this estimate is similar in magnitude to the average within-participant correlation between confidence and response time reported across 4,089 participants from 76 datasets in the Confidence Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Rahnev et al., 2020)</ref>, r = -.24.

text.text: Together, these results indicate that the LLM ratings provide valid, scalable proxies for human judgments of the five dimensions, supporting their use across the full verbalization corpus.
Finally, we examined whether categories generated without specifying the four deliberation functions corresponded to our function scores.
We used a different LLM (DeepSeek V4 Flash; DeepSeek-AI, 2026) to label the primary reasoning operation expressed in each chunk, without providing the four functions or their definitions.
text.formatted: We used a different LLM <ref type="bibr">(DeepSeek V4 Flash;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">DeepSeek-AI, 2026)</ref> to label the primary reasoning operation expressed in each chunk, without providing the four functions or their definitions.

text.text: We then grouped the resulting labels into broader categories in a second automated pass.
For each category, we compared the four deliberation-function scores of its chunks with those of all remaining chunks using standardized mean differences (Cohen's d).
Overall, the bottom-up categories mapped well onto the four deliberation functions.
The prompts, the complete category list, and the detailed comparisons can be found in Supplementary Material 3.
The original dataset contains 1,020 recordings of think-aloud trials (102 participants × 10 items).
Fourteen trials had no audio file in the publicly available data, and five recordings produced unusable transcriptions due to a failure of the speech-to-text model.
Of the 1,001 remaining recordings, 32 failed to yield any chunk that could be matched back to the wordlevel timestamps.
This left 969 successfully scored trials (95.0% of all recordings; 4,011 chunks).
We then applied four additional exclusion criteria.

First, because familiarity strongly predicts performance on the vCRT and a familiar item can be answered from memory rather than reasoned through (Byrd et al., 2023; Stieger & Reips, 2016), we excluded all trials from the 17 participants who mentioned knowing at least one item (163 trials).
text.formatted: First, because familiarity strongly predicts performance on the vCRT and a familiar item can be answered from memory rather than reasoned through <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Byrd et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Stieger & Reips, 2016)</ref>, we excluded all trials from the 17 participants who mentioned knowing at least one item (163 trials).

text.text: Second, because all accuracy analyses contrast correct with biased responses, we excluded 42 of the remaining 806 trials whose response was not coded as such (i.e., unrelated or unclear answers as coded by Byrd et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Second, because all accuracy analyses contrast correct with biased responses, we excluded 42 of the remaining 806 trials whose response was not coded as such (i.e., unrelated or unclear answers as coded by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Third, of the remaining 764 trials, 122 contained only one chunk.

These trials were retained in prevalence analyses examining how often each deliberation function was expressed, but excluded from analyses of deliberation trajectories, which required at least two chunks per trial.
Finally, we found that verbalizations typically opened with a re-reading of the item and closed with a statement of the chosen answer.
We therefore scored two additional dimensions in separate prompts: repetition, defined as the mere repetition of information, and answer selection, defined as stating the chosen answer.

Because these behaviors could distort the estimated deliberation trajectories, we removed edge chunks (first or last 20% of relative time; see Supplementary Material 4 for the choice of these cutoffs) whose highest-scoring dimension was repetition or answer selection and that accounted for more than 60% of the chunk's scores summed across the four deliberation functions and the two auxiliary dimensions (see Supplementary Material 4 for the full rationale), removing 745 of 2,957 chunks.

This filtering left a further 77 trials with fewer than two chunks, which were excluded from analyses of deliberation trajectories, but were included in prevalence analyses of how often each deliberation function was expressed.
Relative time (see below) was recomputed on the retained chunks, such that 0 and 1 correspond to the onset of the first and the offset of the last retained chunk.

To ensure that our conclusions did not depend on this last exclusion criterion, Supplementary Material 4 reports robustness analyses with no edge-chunk filtering at all and with a maximally strict filter removing every edge chunk whose highest-scoring dimension was repetition or answer selection, regardless of its share.
We indicate results that were not robust to these variations in the main text.
The final sample for analyses of deliberation trajectories thus contained 2,141 chunks from 565 trials (268 correct, 297 biased) and 76 participants, that is, 55% of all recordings.
As shown in Figure 2A, the final sample contained an average of 3.8 chunks per trial (SD = 1.9, Mdn = 3, range = 2-15), corresponding to a mean response time of 29.6 s (SD = 19.7).

text.text: All statistical analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2025).

We conducted triallevel comparisons of verbalization length between correct and biased responses with mixedeffects models fitted with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015), each with crossed random intercepts for participant and item: linear mixed models for log-transformed response time and word count, a Poisson generalized linear mixed model for the number of chunks, and a binomial generalized linear mixed model with a logit link for the probability of trial exclusion.
text.formatted: We conducted triallevel comparisons of verbalization length between correct and biased responses with mixedeffects models fitted with the lme4 package <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>, each with crossed random intercepts for participant and item: linear mixed models for log-transformed response time and word count, a Poisson generalized linear mixed model for the number of chunks, and a binomial generalized linear mixed model with a logit link for the probability of trial exclusion.

text.text: Degrees of freedom for the linear models were approximated with Satterthwaite's method (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Degrees of freedom for the linear models were approximated with Satterthwaite's method <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To capture nonlinear time courses, we used generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs), fitted with the mgcv package (Wood, 2017).
text.formatted: To capture nonlinear time courses, we used generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs), fitted with the mgcv package <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Wood, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Each chunk was assigned a single temporal value, the midpoint between its onset and offset.

Because trials varied in length, this midpoint was expressed relative to the span of retained chunks after exclusion and rescaled from 0 (onset of the first retained chunk) to 1 (offset of the last retained chunk), placing all trials on a common relative time scale.

GAMMs model temporal trajectories as smooth functions estimated with penalized regression splines; the degree of smoothness is estimated from the data, allowing flexible nonlinear relationships while preventing overfitting.

GAMMs summarize the shape of each fitted curve by its effective degrees of freedom (edf), where an edf of 1 indicates a linear trajectory, while larger values indicate increasingly complex nonlinear trajectories.

Because the four functions were modeled jointly, random intercepts for participants and items were estimated separately for each function, so that, for example, a participant with a general tendency to justify and an item that rarely elicited control each received their own function-specific baseline.

We also added a per-trial random intercept when it improved fit, because analyses were conducted at the chunk level, and models including accuracy as a predictor additionally included random accuracy slopes for participants and items when supported (Matuschek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: We also added a per-trial random intercept when it improved fit, because analyses were conducted at the chunk level, and models including accuracy as a predictor additionally included random accuracy slopes for participants and items when supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Random-effects structures were compared with approximate likelihood-ratio tests on restricted-maximum-likelihood (REML) fits, and the retained models were refitted using exact REML.

Because the deliberation scores contained many zeros (generation: 23.9%; justification: 58.1%; control: 61.4%; regulation: 63.3%), we used a two-part (hurdle) approach separating each trajectory into two parts: an activation part, modeling whether a function was expressed at all (i.e., had a score > 0) with a binomial GAMM, and an intensity part, modeling how strongly it was expressed among active chunks with a beta GAMM.

text.text: For the beta GAMM, we rescaled the scores to 0-1, and then to the interval [.001, .999], as required by the beta distribution (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006).
text.formatted: For the beta GAMM, we rescaled the scores to 0-1, and then to the interval [.001, .999], as required by the beta distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Because each chunk's score is the average of eight ratings, a single nonzero rating is enough for a chunk to count as active under the score > 0 criterion.
text.formatted: Because each chunk's score is the average of eight ratings, a single nonzero rating is enough for a chunk to count as active under the score > 0 criterion.

text.text: Supplementary Material 4 therefore reports robustness analyses in which activation instead required a score above 5; wherever a result was not robust to this stricter criterion, we indicate it explicitly in the main text.
Both parts included function-specific smooths of relative time and a smooth of the log number of chunks per trial, controlling for trial verbosity.
In accuracy analyses, smooths were estimated separately for each function × accuracy combination.
Confidence (0-100) was analyzed analogously with a beta GAMM.
Fitted trajectories are reported with random effects set to zero (i.e., for an average participant and item), so that curves reflect population-level trajectories.

We report simultaneous 95% confidence intervals computed using the itsadug package (van Rij et al., 2025), which maintain 95% coverage across the entire curve rather than at each time point separately; differences between conditions were computed on the link scale before back-transforming them to the response scale, and we report the periods during which the simultaneous interval of the difference excluded zero.
The full model specifications are reported in Supplementary Material 5.
To examine the temporal relationship between confidence and deliberation, we conducted lagged analyses in both directions.
We first tested whether confidence predicted deliberation at the subsequent chunk.

Chunk confidence was standardized and decomposed into a participant mean, a trial deviation, and a within-trial chunk deviation, isolating moment-tomoment fluctuations from participant-and trial-level differences (Curran & Bauer, 2011); only the within-trial chunk deviation was lagged (chunk n -1).
text.formatted: Chunk confidence was standardized and decomposed into a participant mean, a trial deviation, and a within-trial chunk deviation, isolating moment-tomoment fluctuations from participant-and trial-level differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>; only the within-trial chunk deviation was lagged (chunk n -1).

text.text: Hurdle GAMMs predicted each function's activation and intensity from these components crossed with function.

Since a deliberation function active at one chunk tends to remain active at the next, each model controlled for the same function's value at the previous chunk, so that any effect of prior confidence reflects a change in deliberation rather than inertia.
We estimated these lagged associations as parametric linear effects within GAMMs that also included a smooth of relative time, as well as the random-effects structure described above.
The effect of each confidence component was estimated separately for each function using the package emmeans (Lenth, 2025).
text.formatted: The effect of each confidence component was estimated separately for each function using the package emmeans <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lenth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Within each component (i.e., the lagged chunk deviation, the trial deviation, and the participant mean), the four function-specific p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: Within each component (i.e., the lagged chunk deviation, the trial deviation, and the participant mean), the four function-specific p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For the reverse-direction analysis, we tested whether continuous deliberation scores predicted subsequent confidence.

We standardized and decomposed the four scores in the same way and entered their participant-and trial-level components and lagged chunk deviations jointly in a beta GAMM, controlling for confidence at the previous chunk and including random intercepts for participants and items.

Because confidence and deliberation may both fluctuate with a slowly varying withintrial state, such as momentary engagement or perceived difficulty, a lagged association between them could, in principle, arise without any direct confidence-deliberation relationship.

We therefore simulated datasets preserving the observed trial structure, in which confidence and the deliberation functions were generated from a shared autoregressive latent state with no direct lagged path between them.
Refitting the same models to these data recovered no effect, whereas the same pipeline applied to simulated data containing a genuine lagged effect recovered it.
This suggests that our results are unlikely to simply reflect confidence and deliberation drifting together over the course of a trial (Supplementary Material 6).
We examined whether the way deliberation unfolded within an individual trial contained enough information to predict its accuracy.
Specifically, we asked whether a trial's deliberation dynamics could predict whether the participant gave the correct response or the intuitive, biased response.

Because the GAMMs tested only average differences between these response types, we adopted a complementary machine-learning approach to assess whether trial accuracy could be predicted out of sample for participants and items the model had never encountered (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017).
text.formatted: Because the GAMMs tested only average differences between these response types, we adopted a complementary machine-learning approach to assess whether trial accuracy could be predicted out of sample for participants and items the model had never encountered <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We summarized each trial using 17 features: the mean, linear slope over relative time, and peak position of each of the four deliberation functions; the mean and slope of confidence; and the number of chunks, total response time, and total word count.
Because many of these features are correlated (see Supplementary Material 7), an unregularized logistic regression would risk overfitting and yield unstable coefficients.
We therefore used elastic-net logistic regression (Zou & Hastie, 2005), fitted with the glmnet package (Friedman et al., 2010).
text.formatted: We therefore used elastic-net logistic regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Zou & Hastie, 2005)</ref>, fitted with the glmnet package <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Friedman et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Elastic net combines a lasso penalty, which can set uninformative coefficients to zero, with a ridge penalty, which shrinks coefficients and allows correlated predictors to share weight.
To assess whether prediction generalized to both new participants and new items, we used nested cross-validation, leaving out one participant group and one item at a time.
The outer cross-validation, which evaluated predictions on data excluded from training, paired each of five participant groups with each of the 10 items, yielding 50 training-test splits.
In each split, the model predicted responses to the excluded item from the excluded participant group.
Training used only responses from the other participants to the other items.

The inner cross-validation, which selected the balance between the lasso and ridge penalties and the overall penalty strength, further divided each outer training set into training and validation sets, again excluding both participants and items from training.
We tested 11 mixing values, ranging from ridge alone (0) to lasso alone (1), and 133 penalty strengths from 10⁻⁶ to 100.

We selected the combination that best distinguished correct from biased responses across the pooled inner-validation predictions, as measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC; .50 indicates chance discrimination and 1 indicates perfect discrimination).
Predictors were standardized using means and standard deviations estimated only from the corresponding training data.
We calculated overall AUC from the pooled outer-test predictions and estimated percentile 95% confidence intervals using 2,000 bootstrap samples.

In each sample, we independently resampled participants within their assigned groups and items across the dataset, with replacement, then recalculated AUC using the existing test predictions without refitting the models.
Finally, to summarize the coefficients, we selected regularization settings through crossed cross-validation on the complete sample and fitted a descriptive model using all trials.
We first examined the overall prevalence of each deliberation function across the verbalizations.
Our LLM scoring procedure assigned each function a score from 0 (Not at all present) to 100 (Extremely present; see Methods and Supplementary Material 1).
Participantlevel mean scores are shown in Figure 2B.
text.formatted: Participantlevel mean scores are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2B</ref>.

text.text: Generation scored highest (M = 17.7, SD = 7.0), followed by justification (M = 13.3, SD = 10.0), control (M = 4.8, SD = 4.6), and regulation (M = 2.9, SD = 3.6).
Overall prevalence, however, does not reveal when each function occurs during deliberation.
Nor do average scores distinguish between how often a function is active and how strongly it is expressed when active.
We therefore used hurdle GAMMs to estimate separate temporal trajectories for activation and intensity.
If reasoners produce a candidate answer before evaluating it, generation should be active early in the verbalization, followed by justification and control.
Alternatively, reasoners may first justify their initial response and generate a new one only if this justification fails (Evans, 2019), in which case justification should precede generation.
text.formatted: Alternatively, reasoners may first justify their initial response and generate a new one only if this justification fails <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Evans, 2019)</ref>, in which case justification should precede generation.

text.text: Activation changed significantly over relative time for every function, edf = 10.87 for generation, 10.72 for justification, 4.40 for control, and 1.01 for regulation, all ps < .001 (Figure 2C).
text.formatted: Activation changed significantly over relative time for every function, edf = 10.87 for generation, 10.72 for justification, 4.40 for control, and 1.01 for regulation, all ps < .001 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2C</ref>).

text.text: Generation was active in a large majority of chunks over most of the verbalization before declining sharply near its end, and justification became progressively more active before dropping sharply at the very end as well.
Control activation increased gradually over the verbalization, and regulation rose roughly linearly throughout.
The results of the intensity model are shown in Figure 2D.
text.formatted: The results of the intensity model are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2D</ref>.

text.text: Conditional on being active, generation and justification both changed significantly over relative time, edf = 5.23 and 2.59, both ps < .001.
text.formatted: Conditional on being active, generation and justification both changed significantly over relative time, edf = 5.23 and 2.59, both ps < .001.

text.text: Justification grew steadily stronger and plateaued toward the end of the verbalization, whereas generation increased through most of the reasoning process before declining near the end.
Control and regulation intensity did not change significantly, edf = 1.26 and 1.00, ps = .26 and .44, and remained at a low level throughout.
Together, these results reveal a clear population-level temporal structure in participants' verbalized reasoning.
Generation remained active and grew stronger across most of the verbalization, before declining near the end, whereas justification became both more active and stronger as reasoning progressed.
Control and regulation also became more active toward the end, although their intensity remained low.
Thus, the average temporal profile shifted from a predominance of generation toward a greater contribution of justification and, to a lesser extent, control and regulation.
This result is more consistent with reasoners initially generating a candidate answer before evaluating it than with generation occurring only after an initial attempt at justification has failed.

What set apart a correct response from a biased one?
One possibility is that correct responses involve more verbalized reasoning overall, if participants giving the correct response tend to deliberate more.
Another is that they differ in the functional composition and timing of that reasoning.
We found evidence for both routes.

First, biased trials were more likely than correct trials to provide too little verbalized reasoning to model their temporal trajectory: after preprocessing, 34.0% of biased trials and 14.6% of correct trials retained fewer than two eligible reasoning chunks and were therefore excluded from our trajectory analyses.

A mixed-effects logistic regression with crossed random intercepts for participant and item indicated significantly higher odds of exclusion for biased trials compared to correct ones, OR = 2.20, 95% CI [1.27, 3.83], z = 2.80, p = .005.
Among the trials retained for trajectory analysis, however, we found no evidence that correct and biased responses differed in verbalization length.

Linear mixed-effects models with crossed random intercepts for participant and item indicated no significant difference in logtransformed response time, b = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.07], t(551.78) = -0.24, p = .81, or logtransformed word count, b = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.07], t(533.73) = -0.19, p = .85.

A Poisson generalized linear mixed-effects model with the same random-effects structure likewise provided no evidence that the number of chunks differed by response, b = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.04], z = -1.18, p = .24.
Thus, some biased responses showed limited evidence of deliberation, but among the retained trials, overall verbalization length did not differ detectably by response.
Beyond the amount of verbalized reasoning, correct and biased responses differed descriptively in their functional composition across the broader prevalence sample (Figure 3A).
text.formatted: Beyond the amount of verbalized reasoning, correct and biased responses differed descriptively in their functional composition across the broader prevalence sample (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3A</ref>).

text.text: Participant-level mean generation scores were nearly identical for correct (M = 18.6, SD = 9.1) and biased responses (M = 18.6, SD = 9.3).

By contrast, justification scores were higher for correct (M = 20.5, SD = 16.2) than biased responses (M = 8.9, SD = 9.9), as were control scores (correct: M = 7.9, SD = 6.5; biased: M = 2.6, SD = 4.4).
Regulation showed a smaller difference in the same direction (correct: M = 3.6, SD = 4.1; biased: M = 2.9, SD = 4.7).

We next used trajectory models to examine whether correct and biased responses differed in the activation and intensity of each function over time (see Supplementary Material 8 for the exact periods of statistically significant differences).

The activation model (Figure 3B) showed no difference in the likelihood that generation was activated across correct and biased responses, although generation varied strongly over time in both correct (edf = 8.14, p < .001) and biased trials (edf = 7.40, p < .001).

text.text: Justification was more likely to be activated in correct responses at the beginning and toward the end of the verbalization.
Its trajectory was strongly nonlinear in both correct and biased responses, edf = 8.74 and 6.63, respectively, both ps < .001, with a more pronounced increase toward the end in correct trials.
text.formatted: Its trajectory was strongly nonlinear in both correct and biased responses, edf = 8.74 and 6.63, respectively, both ps < .001, with a more pronounced increase toward the end in correct trials.

text.text: Control was more likely to be activated in correct responses at the beginning and across most of the remainder of the verbalization, while regulation showed a similar pattern.

Both functions showed nonlinear increases in correct trials (control: edf = 6.27; regulation: edf = 3.67, both ps < .001), whereas their trajectories in biased trials were closer to linear (control: edf = 1.61; regulation: edf = 1.09, both ps < .001).

text.text: Generation scores were higher for biased than correct responses during part of the second half of the verbalization, although this difference was small and not consistently robust across exclusion criteria.
Generation intensity varied over time in both correct (edf = 2.23, p = .005) and biased trials (edf = 5.11, p < .001).

text.text: Justification scores were higher for correct than for biased responses from near the beginning through the end of the verbalization and increased nonlinearly in correct trials, with a more pronounced rise through the middle before leveling off near the end (edf = 2.47, p < .001).

text.text: In biased responses, justification increased approximately linearly across time (edf = 1.00, p < .001).

text.text: Control scores were likewise higher for correct responses from near the beginning through the end of the verbalization, although their intensity showed little evidence of systematic temporal change in either correct (edf = 1.88, p = .28) or biased trials (edf = 1.00, p = .42).

We found no evidence of a correct-biased difference for regulation intensity, nor was there evidence of systematic temporal change in either condition (correct: edf = 1.00, p = .87; biased: edf = 1.00, p = .35).
Together, these findings suggest that both correct and biased reasoners may deliberate to generate a solution.
Among the retained trials, we found no evidence that overall verbalization length or the likelihood of generation differed by response.
Correct responses nevertheless showed more frequent activation of justification, control, and regulation, higher justification and control scores, and more pronounced changes in activation over time.
What sets correct and biased responses apart, then, is not whether people deliberate, but what they do during deliberation and when they do it.

Our GAMM analyses showed that correct and biased trials followed systematically different deliberation trajectories.
We next asked whether these differences were sufficiently strong to predict the accuracy of individual trials for participants and items the model had never encountered.
To do so, we used elastic-net logistic regression, which limits overfitting by shrinking the coefficients of weak or redundant predictors.
For each trial, we summarized the mean, slope, and peak position of each deliberation function; the mean and slope of confidence; and the number of chunks, response time, and word count.
The full elastic-net model clearly discriminated correct from biased trials, AUC = .81, 95% CI [.73, .89].
Note.
Retained coefficients from the final elastic-net logistic regression fitted to the complete trajectory-analysis sample.
Predictors were z-standardized.
Coefficients are on the logit scale: positive values predict correct responses and negative values predict biased responses.
As shown in Table 3, the largest positive coefficients were associated with mean control, mean justification, and mean confidence, whereas mean generation predicted biased responses.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>, the largest positive coefficients were associated with mean control, mean justification, and mean confidence, whereas mean generation predicted biased responses.

text.text: Word count also received a negative, although small, coefficient.
Importantly, the model also retained several trajectory features, including the peak positions of control and generation and the slopes of justification and confidence.

Although the full set of features produced stronger discrimination, a model containing only trajectory features (i.e., deliberation function slopes and peak positions, together with confidence slope) still performed above chance, AUC = .66, 95% CI [.58, .74].
These temporal deliberation dynamics therefore carried predictive information in their own right, consistent with the systematic temporal differences identified by the GAMM analyses.
Finally, we divided each trial's verbalization into four equal periods of relative time (i.e., quarters) and fitted a separate predictive model using only the information from each period.
AUC increased across quarters, with confidence intervals excluding chance only in the third and fourth quarters.

Supplementary Material 7 reports these temporal analyses, alongside checks showing that prediction remained above chance without control features, whereas verbalization length alone did not predict accuracy above chance.

Although it has been shown that biased reasoners typically show some metacognitive sensitivity to their errors-reporting lower confidence when they give a biased response than when they give a correct one (De Neys et al., 2011; Mata et al., 2013; Thompson & Johnson, 2014)-confidence is usually sampled only once a response has been produced, leaving open how this sensitivity develops while reasoning is still under way.
text.formatted: Although it has been shown that biased reasoners typically show some metacognitive sensitivity to their errors-reporting lower confidence when they give a biased response than when they give a correct one <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Neys et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Mata et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Thompson & Johnson, 2014)</ref>-confidence is usually sampled only once a response has been produced, leaving open how this sensitivity develops while reasoning is still under way.

text.text: In theory, confidence could be largely set early, based on an initial intuitive estimate of whether the emerging response is correct, rise only once a correct solution has been reached, or progressively track accumulating evidence as reasoning unfolds.
We found evidence for this latter pattern (Figure 4A).
text.formatted: We found evidence for this latter pattern (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4A</ref>).

text.text: Correct and biased trials showed no significant difference in confidence early in the verbalization, but their confidence trajectories diverged from relative time .18 onward.
Confidence increased linearly across correct trials, edf = 1.00, p < .001, whereas it tended to decrease linearly in biased trials, although this trend was not significant, edf = 1.00, p = .08.
text.formatted: Confidence increased linearly across correct trials, edf = 1.00, p < .001, whereas it tended to decrease linearly in biased trials, although this trend was not significant, edf = 1.00, p = .08.

text.text: Thus, the confidence advantage for correct responses emerged gradually rather than only once a solution was reached, driven primarily by increasing confidence on correct trials and consistent with confidence progressively tracking evidence for the emerging response.

According to meta-reasoning accounts (Ackerman & Thompson, 2017), confidence and deliberation form a feedback loop in which confidence monitors the ongoing reasoning process and guides the allocation of further cognitive effort, which in turn feeds back into confidence.
text.formatted: According to meta-reasoning accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ackerman & Thompson, 2017)</ref>, confidence and deliberation form a feedback loop in which confidence monitors the ongoing reasoning process and guides the allocation of further cognitive effort, which in turn feeds back into confidence.

text.text: If so, lower confidence within a trial should predict greater activation or intensity of some deliberation functions at the next chunk.
Reciprocally, greater engagement in particular functions should predict higher confidence at the next chunk.
We tested these reciprocal lagged associations across successive chunks.
All coefficients are reported on the logit scale, with response-scale average marginal effects displayed in Figure 4B.

text.text: We first tested whether confidence predicted subsequent deliberation, separately for activation and intensity.

Within trials, confidence at the preceding chunk was negatively associated with subsequent activation of generation, b = -0.52, 95% CI [-0.69, -0.35], p < .001; justification, b = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.16], p < .001; and control, b = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.32, -0.06], p = .007.

text.text: Regulation activation was not reliably associated with prior confidence, b = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.03], p = .13.
For intensity, prior confidence was negatively associated only with subsequent justification intensity, b = -0.23, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.14], p < .001.
text.formatted: For intensity, prior confidence was negatively associated only with subsequent justification intensity, b = -0.23, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.14], p < .001.

text.text: Confidence was not reliably associated with the subsequent intensity of generation, b = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.02], p = .29; control, b = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.11], p = .73; or regulation, b = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.15], p = .35 (see Supplementary Material 9 for the corresponding figure).
Thus, within trials, lower confidence at one chunk was followed by a greater likelihood that generation, justification, and control were active at the next and by stronger justification when active.
