We then tested the association in the reverse direction.
Only regulation showed a reliable lagged association: greater regulation at the preceding chunk was followed by higher confidence at the next, b = 0.11, 95% CI [0.04, 0.17], p = .009.

Generation (b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.04], p = .44), justification (b = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.03], p = .44), and control (b = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.03], p = .44) did not reliably predict subsequent confidence.
Taken together, the bidirectional pattern of lagged associations is consistent with meta-reasoning accounts of the relationship between confidence and deliberation.
Deliberation is central to theories of reasoning, yet we know surprisingly little about what people do once they start thinking a problem through.
Here, we reanalyzed the think-aloud data of Byrd et al. (2023), using LLMs to segment and score successive moments of verbalized reasoning on four deliberation functions, as well as on confidence.
text.formatted: Here, we reanalyzed the think-aloud data of <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Byrd et al. (2023)</ref>, using LLMs to segment and score successive moments of verbalized reasoning on four deliberation functions, as well as on confidence.

text.text: This allowed us to ask which functions reasoners engaged during deliberation, in what order, and how these dynamics related to accuracy and confidence.

Overall, we found a clear population-level temporal organization of deliberation: generation was frequently engaged from the beginning, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly recruited as reasoning progressed.

This early engagement of generation is more consistent with reasoners initially generating a candidate answer than with generation occurring only after an initial justification has failed (Evans, 2019).
text.formatted: This early engagement of generation is more consistent with reasoners initially generating a candidate answer than with generation occurring only after an initial justification has failed <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Evans, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The functions also largely overlapped, with several functions often active within the same verbalization and their relative prevalence shifting over time.
Deliberation may thus be better described as an iteration through complementary functions than as a choice among mutually exclusive ones (De Neys, 2025).
Regarding accuracy, correct and biased responses differed primarily in the functional composition and temporal organization of their deliberation.
Correct responses involved more frequent justification, control, and regulation, as well as stronger justification and control.
Generation did not differ detectably in activation frequency between response types.
Its intensity tended to be slightly higher in biased responses near the end of the verbalizationalthough this difference was not consistent across exclusion criteria.
An elastic-net classifier confirmed that these differences were strong enough to predict the accuracy of individual trials for held-out participants and items.
Thus, reasoning accuracy was distinguished not only by which functions were engaged, but also by how they unfolded over time.
Our temporal trajectory results further showed that control distinguished correct from biased responses both near the beginning of the verbalization and throughout much of its second half.

This pattern is compatible with control serving two distinct roles (De Neys, 2025): early on, inhibiting the intuitive response to allow further deliberation, and later, suppressing that response once an alternative has been generated and the initial answer must be abandoned.
Our findings also clarify the role of justification, which has often been discussed in terms of rationalizing an initial response (Evans & Wason, 1976; Pennycook et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Our findings also clarify the role of justification, which has often been discussed in terms of rationalizing an initial response <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Evans & Wason, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Pennycook et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Justification was both more frequent and more strongly expressed when reasoning succeeded.

This pattern complements experimental evidence that asking participants to justify their responses improves reasoning accuracy (Isler et al., 2020; Isler & Yilmaz, 2023), suggesting that justification can causally support correct reasoning.
text.formatted: This pattern complements experimental evidence that asking participants to justify their responses improves reasoning accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Isler et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Isler & Yilmaz, 2023)</ref>, suggesting that justification can causally support correct reasoning.

text.text: Thus, although justification may contribute to biased reasoning in some cases, accounts tying it primarily to biased responding capture only one side of its role (De Neys, 2025).
Most biased trials contained enough deliberation to be analyzed.
Among the trials retained for our trajectory analyses, we found no evidence that correct and biased responses differed in response time, word count, or number of chunks.
What distinguished them was largely how deliberation was functionally organized.

This is consistent with dual-process accounts distinguishing between two routes to a biased response: a failure to engage deliberation and a failure to reach the correct response despite deliberating (Evans, 2019; Pennycook, 2023; Pennycook et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This is consistent with dual-process accounts distinguishing between two routes to a biased response: a failure to engage deliberation and a failure to reach the correct response despite deliberating <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Evans, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Pennycook, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Pennycook et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our results speak primarily to this second route and support the view that biased reasoners may often be thinking in vain rather than simply failing to think (Beucler, Purcell, Charles, De Neys, & Desender, 2026; Markovits et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our results speak primarily to this second route and support the view that biased reasoners may often be thinking in vain rather than simply failing to think <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Beucler, Purcell, Charles, De Neys, & Desender, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Markovits et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because we extracted confidence throughout the verbalizations, we could also trace how it changed as reasoning progressed.
Correct and biased trials showed no detectable confidence difference early in the verbalization, but their confidence trajectories progressively diverged.
Confidence increased reliably during correct trials, whereas it showed only a small, non-reliable tendency to decrease during biased trials.

This extends conflict-detection accounts in the reasoning literature, in which low confidence signals that an intuitive response may be unreliable and prompts further deliberation (De Neys et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This extends conflict-detection accounts in the reasoning literature, in which low confidence signals that an intuitive response may be unreliable and prompts further deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Neys et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Thompson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The trajectories show how confidence came to distinguish correct from biased responses as reasoning progressed.

More broadly, the divergence in confidence is consistent with evidenceaccumulation accounts, in which decisions arise from the gradual integration of evidence for competing responses and confidence reflects the evolving balance of that evidence (Desender et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2015).
text.formatted: More broadly, the divergence in confidence is consistent with evidenceaccumulation accounts, in which decisions arise from the gradual integration of evidence for competing responses and confidence reflects the evolving balance of that evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Desender et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Yu et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our analyses revealed that confidence and deliberation were also dynamically coupled across successive reasoning chunks.
Within trials, locally lower confidence was followed by greater recruitment of generation, justification, and control, as well as stronger justification once it was engaged.
This is consistent with the idea that uncertainty signals the need for further deliberation.
We also examined whether engagement in a deliberation function predicted confidence at the next reasoning chunk.

Only regulation, which involves monitoring and managing one's reasoning and effort, was reliably followed by higher confidence, while generation, justification, and control did not reliably predict subsequent confidence.

Together, these findings suggest a bidirectional relationship between confidence and deliberation during reasoning, consistent with meta-reasoning accounts of the reciprocal interplay between metacognitive monitoring and cognitive control (Ackerman & Thompson, 2017; De Neys, 2023).
text.formatted: Together, these findings suggest a bidirectional relationship between confidence and deliberation during reasoning, consistent with meta-reasoning accounts of the reciprocal interplay between metacognitive monitoring and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ackerman & Thompson, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">De Neys, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our approach also has methodological implications, as combining think-aloud protocols with automated LLM scoring makes it possible to characterize the trajectory of different deliberation functions over the course of reasoning, beyond simply establishing whether a given function occurs during reasoning.

Likewise, the strong agreement between the LLM and the human ratings supports the use of the LLM scores as a measure of expressed confidence, which can be extracted throughout a verbalization without interrupting the reasoning process.
This makes it possible to examine confidence fluctuations within a single reasoning episode and relate them to the reasoning processes occurring immediately before or afterward.

Such scores could therefore complement explicit confidence ratings collected repeatedly during problem solving (e.g., Ackerman, 2014) by providing access to the development of confidence between the moments at which ratings are requested (see also Metcalfe & Wiebe, 1987, who probed feeling of warmth in the same way).
text.formatted: Such scores could therefore complement explicit confidence ratings collected repeatedly during problem solving (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ackerman, 2014)</ref> by providing access to the development of confidence between the moments at which ratings are requested (see also <ref type="bibr">Metcalfe & Wiebe, 1987, who probed</ref> feeling of warmth in the same way).

text.text: Future work could examine how LLM-derived and explicit confidence measures relate to one another and jointly capture changes in confidence during reasoning.
Practically, this approach could help clarify how interventions change reasoning and inform ways to improve it in humans and artificial systems.
Beyond asking whether an instruction increases deliberation, researchers could examine which functions it changes and when.

An instruction to "think carefully," for example, might prolong generation without encouraging subsequent justification or control, helping explain why additional deliberation does not always improve performance.
Tracking these trajectories could inform more targeted training and richer feedback, supporting people's own reasoning rather than supplying a solution.

Someone who repeatedly generates answers without evaluating them, for example, could receive an instruction to justify or reconsider a candidate response at a specific moment determined by their deliberation trajectory.
Similarly, applied to AI-generated reasoning traces, the same framework could reveal whether successful and unsuccessful outputs differ in their functional organization.

Such comparisons could provide more informative evaluations of AI reasoning by identifying patterns associated with correct and incorrect answers, and potentially inform model training and instructions.
These findings should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
Our trajectory analyses required sufficient verbalized reasoning to estimate changes over time.
Biased trials were more likely than correct trials to be excluded on this basis, so responses with little verbalized reasoning are underrepresented in the retained sample.

Our findings therefore primarily characterize reasoning episodes in which participants engaged in deliberation, but they do not establish whether a response was initially generated intuitively, regardless of whether it was correct or biased.
The present account of deliberation also depended on the categories used to score the verbalizations, as we explicitly supplied the model with the four functions.
In the open-ended labeling analysis (see Supplementary Material 3), a different LLM identified reasoning operations without receiving the four functions or their definitions.
The correspondence between the resulting categories and the function scores provides further support for the taxonomy we used.
However, it does not establish that these functions capture the full range of operations involved in reasoning.
A related caveat concerns the human ratings used to validate the LLM scores.
Although agreement was high overall, the relationship between human and LLM scores was not always linear, and the two may also use the rating scale differently (Li et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although agreement was high overall, the relationship between human and LLM scores was not always linear, and the two may also use the rating scale differently <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Li et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A given LLM score should therefore not be interpreted as directly equivalent to the same numerical rating from humans.
Despite offering a moment-to-moment view of reasoning, our findings should not be interpreted as establishing causal relationships between the processes involved.
For instance, although we observed systematic differences in deliberation functions between correct and biased trials, we cannot conclude that these functions causally influence accuracy.
Similarly, the lagged associations between confidence and deliberation do not establish that either process causally influences the other.

In this respect, combining experimental manipulations with similar fine-grained automated scoring of think-aloud protocols may be particularly fruitful for testing hypotheses about when and why particular deliberation functions are engaged.
Overall, the present study shows that deliberation is not a single process, but rather involves different functions that become more or less prominent over the course of reasoning.
Generation predominated from the outset, while correct responses were distinguished by more frequent justification, control, and regulation, as well as stronger justification and control.
Confidence was also linked to these dynamics, with locally lower confidence preceding the engagement of several functions and regulation preceding higher confidence.
Understanding deliberation therefore requires asking not only whether people deliberate, but what they do while deliberating and how this changes from one moment to the next.
The current findings indicate that characterizing these dynamics is a key step toward opening the "black box" (De Neys, 2025; Myers & Chater, 2024) of human-and potentially artificial-deliberation.
text.formatted: The current findings indicate that characterizing these dynamics is a key step toward opening the "black box" (De Neys, 2025; Myers & Chater, 2024) of human-and potentially artificial-deliberation.

text.text: LLM Prompts and Settings
To segment the verbalization into successive chunks, we used GPT-5.1 with the following parameters: no reasoning effort, temperature = 0 and top-p = 1.
We used the following prompt:
You are an expert in cognitive psychology and verbal protocol analysis.
You are given a transcription of a participant thinking aloud while solving a problem.
Your task is to segment this transcription into meaningful chunks.
A chunk should correspond to a coherent idea, thought, or step in the participant's reasoning or verbal expression -including hesitations, repetitions, or meta-comments.
The goal is not only to segment explicit reasoning steps but to preserve the full structure of the verbalization.
Guidelines: -Do not remove or suppress any part of the original text.
-Do not segment based on arbitrary word count or length.
-Split only when the participant clearly moves to another distinct thought, idea, or reasoning step (e.g., shifting from generating an answer to justifying it, or reflecting on their uncertainty).
-Be conservative in splitting: avoid unnecessary fragmentation.
-Preserve the original wording exactly in each chunk.
Provide your output strictly in the following structure: Chunk 1: [exact text of chunk 1] Chunk 2: [exact text of chunk 2] Chunk 3: [exact text of chunk 3] Be exhaustive.
Here is the transcription to chunk: [transcription]
To score each chunk, we used GPT-5.1 with the following parameters: low reasoning effort, temperature = 1, top-p = 1, n = 8 (i.e., 8 independent completions, averaged for the final score).
For our four deliberation functions, we used the following prompt:
You are an expert in cognitive psychology.
You are given a short chunk of a participant's think-aloud transcription during a reasoning task.
Your task is to rate how strongly this chunk expresses each of the following deliberation functions.

Definitions: -Response Control: Refers to deliberately inhibiting, stopping, or correcting a response judged inappropriate (e.g., self-interruption, "wait/but/actually", rejecting an impulsive answer).
A brief "no/stop" alone is not sufficient unless it clearly halts/corrects an emerging response.
-Response Generation: Refers to actively generating new answers through the deliberate computation or mental simulation of solutions to a given problem.
It often involves hypothetical thinking, algorithmic reasoning, or systematically working through steps to find solutions to a problem.
-Response Justification: Refers to deliberately seeking explicit reasons, arguments, or rationalizations to support or scrutinize generated answers.
It entails building explanations that clarify, validate or invalidate one's judgments.
It often involves giving reasons, referencing evidence, or explaining why an option makes sense or not.
-Response Regulation: Refers to deliberately monitoring and managing one's own cognitive processes by allocating effort and resources strategically.
It often involves reflective decisions about continuing or stopping deliberation, adjusting cognitive investment, or evaluating progress and coherence.
-Each score should reflect the extent to which the chunk expresses the function using a continuous scale from 0 (not at all present) to 100 (extremely present).
-These functions are distinct, but not mutually exclusive -a chunk might score highly on multiple functions if they co-occur.
-If the chunk expresses a completely different kind of function (not captured by the 4 above), do not mention it.
-Do not explain or justify the scores even if the chunk clearly expresses a different kind of function.
Output strictly in this structure (and nothing else):
Here is the question the participant was solving: [question text]
The incorrect, intuitive answer is: [lure answer] The correct answer is: [correct answer]
Here is the current chunk of the transcription: [chunk text]
For the two auxiliary dimensions, the User prompt was the same, but the System prompts were the following:
Repetition:
You are an expert in cognitive psychology.
You are given a short chunk of a participant's think-aloud transcription during a reasoning task.
Your task is to assess the presence of the following behavior:
Repetition refers to the mere repetition of information -such as repeating the question or response options.
Instructions: -Score how strongly this behavior is present on a scale from 0 (not at all present) to 100 (extremely present).
-If the chunk contains no trace of this behavior, assign 0.
This is perfectly acceptable.
-Output only the numeric score, no explanation.
You are an expert in cognitive psychology.
You are given a short chunk of a participant's think-aloud transcription during a reasoning task.
Your task is to assess the presence of the following behavior:
Answer Selection refers to the participant selecting their chosen response option.
Instructions: -Score how strongly this behavior is present on a scale from 0 (not at all present) to 100 (extremely present).
-If the chunk contains no trace of this behavior, assign 0.
This is perfectly acceptable.
-Output only the numeric score, no explanation.
Finally, for confidence, the prompt was the following; importantly, the model was given neither the current question nor the correct or incorrect responses:
You are given a short chunk of a participant's think-aloud reasoning.
Estimate how confident the speaker sounds in this passage -based on how committed they seem to their ideas, how certain they appear, and whether they express doubt or hesitation.
Instructions: -Give a score between 0 (not confident at all) and 100 (extremely confident).
-If you are uncertain, choose a midpoint score around 50.
-Output only the numeric score.

text.text: In the human validation, seven human raters (the two authors and five colleagues working on dual-process theories in reasoning) scored a common sample of 99 chunks (we initially sampled 100, but removed one duplicated chunk), covering the full range of scores for each function and confidence.
Raters first scored confidence based on the chunk alone.
They then rated the four deliberation functions with the reasoning problem and the correct and intuitive answers provided as context.
The instructions were as follows:

You will be given short chunks of a participant's think-aloud transcription during a reasoning task (they typed their responses into text boxes while being audio-recorded as they verbalized their thoughts).
Estimate how confident the speaker sounds in this passage based on how committed they seem to their ideas, how certain they appear, and whether they express doubt or hesitation.
-Rate the participant's confidence on a continuous scale from 0 (Not confident at all) to 100 (Extremely confident).

You will be given short chunks from a participant's think-aloud transcription during a reasoning task (they typed their responses into text boxes while being audio-recorded as they verbalized their thoughts).
Your task is to rate how strongly each chunk expresses the following deliberation functions:
Refers to deliberately inhibiting or suppressing a generated response when it is deemed inappropriate for the given context.
It often involves avoiding immediate reaction or blocking a response.
Refers to actively generating new answers through deliberate computation or mental simulation of solutions to a given problem.
It often involves hypothetical thinking, algorithmic reasoning, or systematically working through steps to find solutions to a problem.
Refers to deliberately seeking explicit reasons, arguments, or rationalizations to support or scrutinize generated answers.
It entails building explanations that clarify, validate or invalidate one's judgments.
It often involves giving reasons, referencing evidence, or explaining why an option makes sense or not.
Refers to deliberately monitoring and managing one's own cognitive processes by allocating effort and resources strategically.
It often involves reflective decisions about continuing or stopping deliberation, adjusting cognitive investment, or evaluating progress and coherence.
-Rate each function separately for each chunk, using a continuous scale from 0 (Not at all present) to 100 (Extremely present).
-These functions are distinct but not mutually exclusive.
A chunk might score highly on multiple functions simultaneously.
-If a chunk does not show any of these functions, assign 0 to all functions.
This is perfectly acceptable.
-If a chunk expresses a completely different kind of function (not listed above), simply do not score or mention it.
-Do not provide explanations or justifications for your scores.
We next identified the model, prompt, and settings whose scores best matched the averaged human ratings.
We varied three dimensions: the model, the prompting strategy, and, for the selected model, the reasoning-effort setting.
Throughout, the labels in parentheses correspond to the configurations shown in Figure S1.

text.text: We first compared two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-5.1.

For the prompting strategy, we contrasted a unified prompt, in which a single call scored all four deliberation functions simultaneously ("Llama -base prompt"), with an individual strategy that scored each function in a separate call ("Llama -one call per function").

We then refined the unified prompt, which performed better than the individual strategy, over successive versions: we broadened the definition of Control to include the interruption and correction of an emerging response, such as "wait," "but," or "actually" ("Llama -broader Control def." and "GPT -broader Control def."); removed an instruction requiring all four scores to be zero when no function was present ("GPT -no forced-zero rule"); specified that partial or incomplete solution attempts still counted as Generation ("GPT -partial generation counts"); and added brief low-, moderate-, and high-intensity examples for each function ("GPT -with scoring examples").

(2023) hand-coded from the same verbalizations: whether the participant verbally reconsidered their initial response and whether they verbalized reasons for or against a response.

As an open-ended, taxonomy-independent check, we used DeepSeek V4 Flash to assign one primary operation to each chunk.
We used a two-pass approach: in the first pass, the LLM had to identify the primary reasoning operation of each chunk.
In the second pass, the LLM was given labels from the first pass occurring at least three times, with examples, and had to merge the categories to obtain fewer categories.
The LLM then assigned each label from the first pass to the newly created categories from the second pass.
All calls used temperature 0 and top-p 1.
The first pass used a maximum of 800 tokens and no reasoning effort.
The first stage of the second pass used a "low" reasoning effort with a maximum of 16,000 tokens, while the second stage used no reasoning effort with a maximum of 1,500 tokens.
A participant is thinking aloud while solving the following reasoning problem:
Here is one short passage from their verbalization:
Your task is to identify the primary reasoning operation the participant performs in this passage: the main step they take in reasoning toward an answer to the problem.
These recordings come from participants deliberating aloud, so most identifiable operations are steps in that deliberation.
Instructions: -Give a single label, a singular noun of one or two words (e.g., "Calculation", not "Calculating").
-The label must name an operation the participant performs on the problem or on their own thinking.
If your label would fit almost any sentence anyone could utter, it is too vague.
Avoid labels that merely name a form of speech, such as Comment, Statement, Observation, Expression, Response, Reaction, Remark, or Description; give a more specific operation, or return None.
-Be as precise as the passage allows.
A label that would fit any step of deliberation carries no information: prefer one that distinguishes this passage from other passages in which the participant is also reasoning.
-Avoid overly generic labels that merely restate that the participant is thinking; name the particular operation instead.
Where one noun would be too broad, use a two-word noun phrase that pins the operation down.
-Use "Repetition" whenever the passage is essentially nothing but the problem's own wording, or a close paraphrase of it.
Use "Answer" when the passage is essentially nothing but the chosen answer.
-Some passages are directed at the participant's own progress rather than at the problem.
Name that operation too, and prefer it over "Repetition" when the passage announces a decision about reading rather than reproducing the problem's wording.
-Describe the operation performed by the participant, never what the problem is about.
-Do not evaluate the participant's reasoning normatively (e.g., as correct, incorrect, good, poor, biased).
In particular, do not label an operation as mistaken (e.g., "Misreading", "Misinterpretation"), but name the operation itself.
-For some passages, no operation is identifiable.
For those the correct answer is None.
A passage can be short and still carry an operation, especially when it concerns the participant's own progress.
Do not explain your choice.
Return only the label on a single line, nothing else.
If no operation is identifiable, return only: None

For instance, correction and rejection load on control, and self-cutoffs to limit the contribution of reading and answer statements to the estimated deliberation trajectories.
Because the choice of cutoffs remains somewhat arbitrary, we tested whether our results depended on this exclusion rule.

We first re-ran the GAMM analyses under two alternative exclusion rules: no edgechunk filtering, and a stricter rule removing every chunk in the first or last 20% of relative time whose highest-scoring dimension was repetition or answer selection, regardless of its share of the total score.
These alternative analyses allowed us to examine whether retaining all edge chunks or excluding more of them changed the results.
Because each LLM score was averaged across eight ratings, a single nonzero rating could otherwise be enough for a function to count as active.
In an additional analysis, we therefore kept the original exclusion rule unchanged, but defined activation as a score above 5 instead of above 0.
This analysis tested whether our results depended on treating very low scores as activation.
In these analyses, the conditional intensity value was in turn estimated only among chunks with scores above 5.
Figures S9 and S10 show the overall activation and intensity trajectories under the original rule and the three alternative robustness analyses.
text.formatted: Figures <ref type="figure">S9</ref> and <ref type="figure">S10</ref> show the overall activation and intensity trajectories under the original rule and the three alternative robustness analyses.

text.text: Results showed that the main temporal patterns were similar across these analyses.
Generation remained the most frequently active function, while justification, control, and regulation generally became more active as the verbalization progressed.
Generation and justification also tended to increase in intensity over much of the verbalization, whereas control and regulation intensity remained comparatively stable.
As expected, requiring a score above 5 lowered activation probabilities and raised conditional intensity, because the weakest scores no longer counted as active.

text.text: One concern in our lagged analyses is that confidence could predict deliberation (or the reverse) simply because both reflect a latent state that simultaneously lowers confidence and increases deliberation.
If this state persists across chunks, low confidence at one chunk could then predict greater deliberation at the next, even in the absence of a direct relationship between them.
We used simulations to test whether our lagged activation model could distinguish this shared-cause pattern from a genuine lagged effect.
In the simulations, we retained the observed participants, items, trials, chunk counts, and relative chunk positions from our data.
Within each trial, we then simulated an unobserved uncertainty state following a first-order autoregressive process (ρ = .50), such that its value partly carried over from one chunk to the next.
We specified confidence to decrease with this state (loading = -0.50; Gaussian noise SD = 0.80), whereas each function's activation probability increased with it (logit loading = 0.50).
Here, we focus on the confidence-todeliberation activation models, but the same logic may extend to the intensity models and to the reverse deliberation-to-confidence models.
Baseline activation rates were taken from the observed data.
In the shared-state-only condition, confidence had no direct lagged effect on activation.
Any effect detected by our analysis pipeline in this condition would therefore constitute a false positive.

In the second condition, confidence at the preceding chunk, expressed as a deviation from that trial's mean, additionally predicted control, generation, and justification activation with a coefficient of -0.30 on the logit scale.
Regulation retained a coefficient of zero and served as a control.
Figure S13 illustrates the two conditions using the same underlying uncertainty and confidence trajectories.

We first examined how repetition and answer selection varied over the course of the verbalization.
We fitted a beta generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) to these two scores before edge-chunk exclusion, with separate smooths of relative time and random intercepts for participants and items.
As shown in Figure S7, repetition was strongest at the beginning of the verbalization, whereas answer selection was strongest toward the end.

text.text: We therefore defined edge chunks as those whose midpoint fell in the first or last 20% of relative time.

We then examined the edge chunks whose highest-scoring dimension was repetition or answer selection.
For each chunk, we divided that score by the sum of the scores across the four deliberation functions, as well as answer selection and question repetition.

To examine how predictive information varied over the verbalization, we divided each trial into four equal quarters of relative time after edge-chunk exclusion.
Chunks were assigned by their midpoint, and a separate elastic-net model was fitted to each quarter.
Each model used eight features: the five mean scores (four deliberation functions and confidence), number of chunks, response time, and word count within that quarter.
We excluded slopes and peak positions because the quarters often contained too few chunks to estimate them reliably.

Each model used only its own quarter, without accumulating information from earlier quarters, and followed the same nested validation procedure, retaining the same participant assignments to outer groups.
A trial contributed only when that quarter contained at least one chunk midpoint.
The number of trials therefore varied across quarters (Table S11).

text.text: Here we visualize the within-trial associations between lagged confidence (at the previous chunk) and the intensity of each deliberation function at the next chunk.
Higher previous confidence was associated with lower subsequent justification intensity, while the associations for generation, control, and regulation were not statistically significant.
Figure 2.
Distribution and overall trajectories of deliberation across relative time.
(A) Distribution of the number of chunks per trial.

(B) Distribution of function scores across participants, where each observation is one participant's mean score for that function on the 0-100 scale.Violins show the full distribution, boxes the median and interquartile range, and diamonds the mean.
(C) Predicted probability that each function is active (i.e., score above zero).

Generation is active from the first retained chunks and remains the most frequently active function throughout, whereas justification, control, and regulation become progressively more likely as the trial unfolds.
(D) Predicted score for each function when it is active.
Justification increases substantially once active, while generation rises over most of the trial before declining near its end; control and regulation remain comparatively low and stable.
